Circuit. An electrical circuit is a closed loop of conducting material—wires and components—through which electric current flows, driven by a voltage source and controlled by resistances, capacitances, and inductances. Circuits are the foundation of all electronic devices, from household appliances to smartphones, and their behavior is governed by fundamental laws—Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws—that relate voltage, current, and resistance.

A circuit requires a complete path for current to flow. An open circuit, or broken path, stops current. A short circuit, or low resistance path, causes excessive current and heat. Voltage is the electrical potential difference driving current. Current is the flow rate of charge. Resistance opposes flow. Ohm's law relates them: voltage equals current times resistance.

Series circuits have components one after another. Current is the same everywhere, but voltages add up. Parallel circuits have branches. Voltage is the same across branches, but currents add. Kirchhoff's laws formalize circuit analysis. Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the sum of voltages around a loop is zero. Kirchhoff's current law states that the sum of currents entering a junction equals currents leaving.

Capacitors store charge. Inductors store energy in magnetic fields. Resistors dissipate energy as heat. Each impedes current flow differently. AC circuits, or alternating current circuits, and DC circuits, or direct current circuits, behave differently. AC circuits involve impedance—frequency-dependent resistance—and power factors describing efficiency.

Resistance reflects the fundamental property of materials to oppose electron flow. Metals are good conductors with low resistance. Rubber and glass are insulators with very high resistance. Circuit topology matters. Changing from series to parallel dramatically alters circuit behavior. Real-world circuits often mix series and parallel sections. Transient behavior occurs when circuits switch on or off. Capacitors and inductors resist instantaneous changes, creating charging and discharging curves and oscillations.
